The user asked for: **Target: AAAI 2026
Track: AI Alignment / Main Technical Track — Robustness Evaluation

Direction: Build an end-to-end framework (CRADE) that jointly profiles per-instance contamination, generates adversarial functional variants with provable correctness, evaluates reasoning at the step level, and produces IRT-calibrated "genuine capability" scores that decompose observed performance into true ability, contamination boost, and robustness deficit. The core insight is that contamination and robustness are entangled — a model may fail perturbations because it memorized answers OR because it lacks genuine reasoning, and disentangling these requires joint modeling that no existing work provides.

Seed Papers:
- Zawalski et al. "CoDeC" (NVIDIA, arXiv 2025) — Gray-box contamination detection at 99.9% AUC; provides the detection backbone but produces no corrective evaluation
- Li et al. "ATLAS" (arXiv 2025) — IRT-based adaptive testing achieving 90% item reduction; demonstrates IRT's power for LLM evaluation but assumes test integrity
- Hou et al. "MaSTer" (arXiv 2026) — Automated adversarial math variant generation with 48% accuracy reduction; best current perturbation method but disconnected from contamination
- Zheng et al. "ReasoningMath-Plus" (arXiv 2026) — Step-level evaluation showing answer-level overestimates by ~1.4 points; proves process-level matters but lacks adversarial component
- Chen et al. "Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think" (Anthropic, May 2025) — CoT faithfulness is only 25% for hint disclosure; establishes that CoT is unreliable but doesn't connect to contamination
- Xu et al. "DCR" (arXiv 2025) — Contamination-adjusted scores via fuzzy inference; closest competitor but lacks IRT grounding, variant generation, and process-level analysis
- Kocetkov et al. "On The Fragility of Benchmark Contamination Detection in Reasoning Models" (arXiv Oct 2025) — Shows detection fails for reasoning models; establishes urgent need for new approaches

Known Gaps:
- No framework jointly estimates contamination level, generates adversarial variants, and produces a single calibrated capability score (existing work addresses these in isolation)
- Step-level perturbation alignment (whether CoT appropriately tracks problem changes) has never been measured or connected to contamination — all adversarial work evaluates final answers only
- Item Response Theory for LLM evaluation (ATLAS, PSN-IRT) assumes zero contamination; contamination-aware IRT with joint ability-contamination estimation is entirely missing
- Existing contamination detection fails on reasoning models (near random-guess), creating demand for process-level and faithfulness-based alternatives

Theoretical Anchor: Contamination-aware 3PL IRT model: P(correct | θ_j, d_i, c_ij) = c_ij · p_mem + (1 - c_ij) · σ(θ_j - d_i), with EM-based joint estimation of ability θ, difficulty d, and contamination indicators c. The decomposition Observed_accuracy = G + C - R (genuine capability + contamination boost - robustness deficit) provides a formal framework grounded in measurement theory.

Constraints:
- Compute: ≤200 H100-hours (estimated ~120 for combined RQ1+RQ2)
- Timeline: 8-10 weeks to AAAI deadline (abstract July 25, paper August 1)
- Must validate calibrated scores against MathArena's uncontaminated 2025 competition data as ground truth

Quality Self-Checks:
- [x] Core insight: "Contamination and robustness are entangled — you can't measure one without accounting for the other, and disentangling them requires joint modeling at the reasoning-step level."
- [x] Why not obvious: The contamination-detection and adversarial-robustness communities are separate research streams with different venues and different authors; the IRT-for-LLMs community is a third silo. Nobody sits at the three-way intersection. DCR Factor shows the field is approaching this but only from the detection+adjustment angle.
- [x] Baseline fear test: A simple baseline of "run on variants and average" loses the contamination-robustness decomposition and the step-level memorization signatures — the calibrated IRT score and process-level SPA metric are what differentiate.
- [x] Information exploited: Per-instance contamination profiles crossed with per-variant step-level reasoning chain changes — no existing method uses this joint signal.

Avoid:
- Pure contamination detection without corrective evaluation (saturated space with 5+ strong methods)
- Yet another dynamic benchmark (LiveBench, MathArena, DyVal already exist) — this must be a framework applicable to ANY existing benchmark
- Ad-hoc perturbation studies on single benchmarks without methodological/theoretical contribution (GSM-Plus, GSM-Symbolic, MATH-Perturb already cover this)
- Using LLMs in the variant generation loop (creates circular dependency and unverifiable correctness) — use SymPy-backed symbolic generation instead**

## The PSN-IRT Framework

PSN-IRT is an enhanced Item Response Theory framework that incorporates a rich set of item parameters within an IRT-grounded architecture. PSN-IRT processes model identifiers and item identifiers through independent neural network pathways that respectively estimate latent model ability and a rich set of item parameters.

## Key Research Findings

The evaluation covered 12 LLMs on 11 benchmarks, totaling 41,871 items. The analysis revealed significant and varied shortcomings in the measurement quality of the 11 LLM benchmarks. Specific issues identified include:

- LLM benchmarks suffer from widespread saturation and insufficient difficulty ceilings, limiting their ability to challenge and accurately evaluate advanced models
- LLM benchmarks exhibit data contamination in numerous items, compromising their reliability

The research demonstrates that leveraging PSN-IRT is able to construct smaller benchmarks while maintaining stronger alignment with human preference.

The Data Contamination Risk (DCR) framework is a lightweight, interpretable pipeline designed to detect and quantify benchmark data contamination (BDC) risk across four granular levels: semantic, informational, data, and label.

The paper discusses how leaderboards for large reasoning models have turned evaluation into a competition, with developers optimizing directly on benchmark suites, and notes that a shortcut to achieving higher rankings is to incorporate evaluation benchmarks into the training data, yielding inflated performance known as benchmark contamination.

The key finding of the paper is that evading contamination detections for LRMs is alarmingly easy, despite numerous contamination detection approaches having been proposed. The researchers found that while contamination during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can be identified by contamination detection methods, even brief GRPO training can markedly conceal contamination signals that most detection methods rely on.

## RIDE: Difficulty Evolving Perturbation with Item Response Theory for Mathematical Reasoning

Large language models (LLMs) achieve high performance on mathematical reasoning, but these results can be inflated by training data leakage or superficial pattern matching rather than genuine reasoning. To address this, an adversarial perturbation-based evaluation is needed to measure true mathematical reasoning ability.

Current rule-based perturbation methods often generate ill-posed questions and impede the systematic evaluation of question difficulty and the evolution of benchmarks. To bridge this gap, RIDE is a novel adversarial question-rewriting framework that leverages Item Response Theory (IRT) to rigorously measure question difficulty and to generate intrinsically more challenging, well-posed variations of mathematical problems.

**Methodology:**

The approach employs 35 LLMs to simulate students and build a difficulty ranker from their responses. This ranker provides a reward signal during reinforcement learning and guides a question-rewriting model to reformulate existing questions across difficulty levels.

**Results:**

Applying RIDE to competition-level mathematical benchmarks yields perturbed versions that degrade advanced LLM performance, thereby exposing limited robustness in mathematical reasoning and confirming the validity of the evaluation approach.

The paper was published on arXiv (2511.04120) in January 2026.

## Overview

MATH-Perturb is an ICML 2025 paper that benchmarks LLMs' math reasoning abilities against hard perturbations. The work investigates whether LLMs have true generalizable mathematical reasoning capability or are merely memorizing problem-solving skills, presenting MATH-Perturb with modified level-5 problems from the MATH dataset to benchmark LLMs' generalizability to slightly perturbed problems.

## Dataset Structure

The researchers construct MATH-P-Simple and MATH-P-Hard via simple perturbation and hard perturbation, respectively, with each consisting of 279 perturbed math problems derived from level-5 (hardest) problems in the MATH dataset.

The simple perturbation to the problem is non-essential, so the modified problem can be solved using the same method as the original problem, while the hard perturbation changes the problem fundamentally and requires more difficult problem-solving skills.

## Answer Verification Using SymPy

The evaluation script extracts the answers within \boxed{}, post-processes the potentially unformatted answer string, and then utilizes the SymPy package to check the equivalence of two latex strings. The approach first performs string normalization and then uses the sympy package to check the equivalence of two mathematical objects.

## Key Findings

The researchers observe significant performance drops on MATH-P-Hard across various models, including o1-mini (-16.49%) and gemini-2.0-flash-thinking (-12.9%). They also raise concerns about a novel form of memorization where models blindly apply learned problem-solving skills without assessing their applicability to modified contexts, with this issue amplified when using original problems for in-context learning.

## ConStat: Performance-Based Contamination Detection (NeurIPS 2024)

ConStat is a statistical test designed to reliably detect and quantify contamination by comparing primary and reference benchmark performance relative to reference models.

### Key Approach

The paper proposes a novel definition of contamination as artificially inflated and non-generalizing benchmark performance instead of the inclusion of benchmark samples in the training data. This perspective enables detection of any model with inflated performance, i.e., performance that does not generalize to rephrased samples, synthetic samples from the same distribution, or different benchmarks for the same task.

### Performance and Results

ConStat detects 89.1% of syntax-specifically contaminated models and identifies 98.4% of sample-specifically contaminated models. The method shows excellent predictiveness with a coefficient of determination (r²) of 0.94 when comparing its estimated sample-specific contamination effect to ground truth measurements.

The research found high levels of contamination in multiple popular models including Mistral, Llama, Yi, and the top-3 Open LLM Leaderboard models.

This is a NeurIPS 2024 paper that presents a statistical test for detecting and quantifying benchmark contamination in LLMs.

## Overview

LEGO-IRT stands for Language model Evaluation under General Outcomes based on Item Response Theory, a framework developed for evaluating Large Language Models.

## Key Features

LEGO-IRT is a unified framework for data-efficient LLM evaluation that overcomes the limitations of prior item response theory (IRT) approaches and uniquely supports both binary and continuous metrics natively, eliminating the need for information-losing discretization.

LEGO-IRT extends contemporary IRT frameworks by introducing factorized designs that effectively decompose model ability estimates into a general component plus structure-specific offsets that properly handle scenarios where multiple metrics or multiple benchmarks are involved.

## Practical Benefits

LEGO-IRT provides stable capability estimates using as little as 3% of the full evaluation data.

## Problem It Addresses

While Item Response Theory (IRT) offers a promising path toward data-efficient evaluation by disentangling model capability from item difficulty, existing IRT-based methods are hampered by significant limitations - they are typically restricted to binary correctness metrics, failing to natively handle the continuous scores used in generative tasks, and they operate on single benchmarks, ignoring valuable structural knowledge.

The framework was published in October 2025 according to the source metadata.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about PaCoST:

## Overview

PaCoST (Paired Confidence Significance Testing) is a novel approach designed for the detection of benchmark contamination in open-source LLMs.

## The Problem It Addresses

Benchmark contamination occurs when benchmarks for LLM evaluation are inadvertently or deliberately included in model training. This inclusion can lead to cheatingly high scores on model leaderboards, yet result in disappointing performance in real-world applications.

## How PaCoST Works

The method constructs a counterpart for each piece of data with the same distribution, and performs statistical analysis of the corresponding confidence to test whether the model is significantly more confident under the original benchmark. The method operates under the assumption that the model tends to demonstrate greater confidence when responding to questions it has been trained on.

## Key Results

When validated on popular open-source models and benchmarks, the researchers found that almost all models and benchmarks they tested were suspected to be contaminated more or less.

## Publication

PaCoST was published in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024, pages 1794–1809.

# Paper Analysis

## Full Abstract

"Public benchmarks increasingly govern how large language models (LLMs) are ranked, selected, and deployed. We frame this benchmark-centered regime as Silicon Bureaucracy and AI Test-Oriented Education, and argue that it rests on a fragile assumption: that benchmark scores directly reflect genuine generalization. In practice, however, such scores may conflate exam-oriented competence with principled capability, especially when contamination and semantic leakage are difficult to exclude from modern training pipelines. We therefore propose an audit framework for analyzing contamination sensitivity and score confidence in LLM benchmarks. Using a router-worker setup, we compare a clean-control condition with noisy conditions in which benchmark problems are systematically deleted, rewritten, and perturbed before being passed downstream. For a genuinely clean benchmark, noisy conditions should not consistently outperform the clean-control baseline. Yet across multiple models, we find widespread but heterogeneous above-baseline gains under noisy conditions, indicating that benchmark-related cues may be reassembled and can reactivate contamination-related memory. These results suggest that similar benchmark scores may carry substantially different levels of confidence. Rather than rejecting benchmarks altogether, we argue that benchmark-based evaluation should be supplemented with explicit audits of contamination sensitivity and score confidence."

**IRT usage:** No mention of Item Response Theory in the provided content.

**Paired adversarial items:** No evidence of this approach in the abstract.
